etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Probably originally a compound of 心 (uru, “heart, mind”, vowel-shifted from regular reading ura, cognate with 裏 (ura, “the behind or inside of something”)) + 狭し (sashi, “tight; narrow”, Classical and Old Japanese, cognate and synonym of modern 狭い (semai)), from the sense that something is so overwhelming that one feels pressured to yield or submit in some way.
The earliest texts used this word to mean something more like "overwhelmed by how completely thorough something is (in a positive sense), or by how excessive and repetitive something is (in a negative sense)". Over time, the term was used less and less in a positive sense, and the focus from the late Heian period gradually became a negative sense of oppression and annoyance from something troublesome, repetitive, or overwhelming. Usage then shifted further, such that the term described not the speaker's own internal state, but rather the troublesome quality of the cause of the emotional response.
First cited to works from the early 900s.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From する (suru, “to do”) + と (to, “when, whenever”, temporal particle). Literally, "when doing [whatever came before], then [whatever comes after]".

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨so₂ no₂⟩ → */sənə/ → /sono/
From Old Japanese そ, distal demonstrative root, with の (no) added to form the ordinary adnominal form 'that', as in 'that word', as opposed to the pronoun それ (sore).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Short of 只(ただ)今(いま)、帰(かえ)りました (tadaima, kaerimashita, “I'm back right now”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Phrase consisting of だ (da, “is, are”, copula) + が (ga, nominative particle, also used contrastively after verbs).
が is also used after verbs in this same way to indicate “the previous statement is the case, but...”

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Clipping of とてもかくても (“no matter how, not at all”), used with negative verbs. The sense "very, exceedingly" is a shift from the earlier sense of "no matter how", and was first attested around 1910-1920. Compare 全然.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From the classical upper bigrade verb(バ行上二段活用) のぶ (nobu). Cognate with Japanese 延(の)びる (nobiru).
Development
Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 上(かみ)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (kami nidan katsuyō, “upper bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 上(かみ)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (kami ichidan katsuyō, “upper monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -iru.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 包 is a daiyōji replacing 繃.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From either 裏(うら) (ura, “back, inside”) or 心(うら) (ura, “heart”, by extension, "inner feelings"), and なふ (nau, verb modifier).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *kapyaru.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. Attested in a text from 701. In turn, reconstructed as descending from Proto-Japonic *wonpa.
Likely a compound of 小 (o-, “small, young”) + 母 (ha, “mother”). Compare 叔父 (oji, “uncle”), also likely from 小 (o-) + 父 (chi, “father”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: The 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 向(む)かう (mukau, “to face”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 喜(よろこ)ぶ (yorokobu, “to be pleased, delighted”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Ultimately from Middle Chinese 地位 (MC dijH hwijH). First cited in Japanese to a text from the mid-1200s, so possibly a learned borrowing from Chinese 地位 (dìwèi).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/tapu/ → /taɸu/ → */tawu/ → /tau/ → /tɔː/ → /toː/
From Middle Chinese 塔 (MC thap, “tower, pagoda, spire”).
An abbreviation for 卒塔婆 (sotoba, sotōba), a transliteration of Sanskrit स्तूप (stūpa, “heap”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: First appears in the Engishiki compilation of laws created in the early 900s, spelled phonetically in kanji as 阿良良伎. Spelled as 蘭, araragi literally means “wild onion” and refers to the wild rocambole, possibly hardneck garlic, notable for its tall green stalk sticking straight up. Used as a euphemism for 塔 (tafu at the time), as that word's Buddhist connotations were viewed as taboo in contexts having to do with the religious center of Itsuki no Miya (斎宮, also known as Saikū).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese かふ (kapu), in the 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) pattern.
Development
Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.
Cognate with 替(か)える (kaeru), 代(か)える (kaeru) and 換(か)える (kaeru).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. Found in the Kojiki of 712, and included in the Man'yōshū with the phonetic man'yōgana spelling 須 (su). In turn, from Proto-Japonic *su.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From the classical upper bigrade verb(バ行上二段活用) のぶ. Cognate with Japanese 伸(の)びる (nobiru).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 役 (yaku, “service, work, role”) and 割り (wari), the noun form of 割る (waru, “to divide”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 急(きゅう) (kyū, “sudden”) + に (ni, oblique particle).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. Cognate with 憎む (nikumu, “to hate”), 難い (-nikui, “difficult [to do]”, verb suffix).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Ultimately from Middle Chinese 扇子.
First attested in Japanese in the Taiheiki of the late 1300s.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 日(ひ) (hi, “day”) + 付(づ)け (-zuke, “fixing, attaching”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 最(さい) (sai-, “most”) + 低(てい) (tei, “low”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 注 is a daiyōji replacing 註.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/moju/ → /mojeru/ → /moeru/
From classical verb 燃ゆ (moyu).
Development
Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Likely 人(ひと) (hito, “person”) + 見(み) (mi, “see”), in reference to one's own reflection when staring into someone else's eyes. Compare Latin pūpilla, of the same derivation.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese 節 (pusi); attested in the Shin'yaku Kegonkyō Ongi Shiki of 794 as 布之. In turn, from Proto-Japonic *pusi. Possibly derived from Old Japanese 節 (pu).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 節 (MC tset).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/opu pu/ → /opopu/ → /ofofu/ → */owou/ → /oːu/
From the Old Japanese verb 覆(お)ふ (opu, “cover from above”) + ふ (-fu, auxiliary verb modifier, expressing repetition or ongoing state).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 見(み) (mi, “seeing”, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 見(み)る (miru, “to see”)) + 送(おく)る (okuru, “to send”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 駐車(ちゅうしゃ) (chūsha, “(car) parking”) + 場(じょう) (-jō, “place”)
